toural.name: Largo do Toural
toural.short: Guimarães' main square: from a cattle market outside the walls to the city's “drawing room”, renewed in 2012
toural.long: Toural grew out of the cattle fair that filled this ground outside the town walls in the 17th century. In 1791 the council leased a strip along the wall for building, and the houses went up to a plan probably sent from Lisbon: arcades at ground level, tall windows, dormer roofs and wrought-iron balconies. A public garden with an iron bandstand opened here in 1878, and a statue of Afonso Henriques later stood at its centre. In 2011 the 16th-century Renaissance fountain returned to the square, and in 2012, for the European Capital of Culture, the whole space was remodelled and linked to Avenida Alberto Sampaio.
toural.history:
Toural grew up outside the walls. In the 17th century this ground by the town's main gate held a fair for cattle and other goods; the square lay beyond the fortifications, on the way to the castle and the Oliveira monastery, and served at once as a market and a meeting place for the townspeople.

In 1791 the town council leased a plot along the wall for building. The houses went up to a plan probably sent from Lisbon, and from then on the fairground slowly turned into a formal square. The façades gained arcades at ground level, huge windows two storeys high, dormer roofs and fine wrought-iron balconies — the look still known today as the city's “drawing room”.

In the second half of the 19th century a Public Garden enclosed by an iron railing was laid out on the square; it opened in 1878. It came with street furniture in the spirit of the new iron architecture: a bandstand, a urinal, benches and lamps. When the Republic was proclaimed the garden was moved elsewhere, and a statue of Afonso Henriques — the work of Soares dos Reis, 1887 — was placed at the centre of the remodelled Toural. It was later moved to the park by the castle, and an ornate “Artistic Fountain” took its place.

The square's water has a story of its own. A Renaissance fountain with three bowls stood here as early as the 16th century; in 1873 it was moved to Largo Martins Sarmento and only in 2011 did it return to the Toural. In 2012, when Guimarães was European Capital of Culture, the square was remodelled: the later fountain was removed, the old one reinstated, and the space reopened, joined to Avenida Alberto Sampaio.

Today the Toural is the city's main hub. The Neoclassical Basilica of São Pedro faces it, and a short walk away, between the squares of Santiago and Oliveira, stands the old town hall (Antigos Paços do Concelho) with its Gothic arcade, now home to the Museum of Modern Primitive Art. The Gualterianas festivities start here, and this is the handiest place to begin a walk through the historic centre.

The square's name recalls its market past: the Portuguese “toural” echoes touro, “bull”, for cattle were traded here for centuries. In the 19th century, when Guimarães was raised to city status by decree of Queen Maria II on 23 June 1853 and the walls began to come down, the Toural finally merged into the urban fabric: new streets were opened and the old market gave way to a square for parades and festivities. Its ground-floor arcades and huge windows have barely changed since, and they still convey the taste of the 18th century. The square has survived the moving of its garden, the changing of its monuments and the remodelling of 2012, yet it remains the city's “drawing room” — a place of meeting and everyday life for the people of Guimarães. The Gualterianas festivities, town fairs and Christmas lights all happen here; in winter a tree and carousels stand on the square, and in summer the cafés put their tables out under the arcades.
facts: The square grew out of the cattle fair held outside the town walls in the 17th century.
In 1791 the council leased a plot along the wall for building, to a plan probably sent from Lisbon.
The public garden with its iron bandstand opened on the square in 1878.
The Renaissance three-bowl fountain returned to the Toural in 2011, after standing on Largo Martins Sarmento since 1873.
The statue of Afonso Henriques stood on the Toural before being moved to the castle in 1940.
The square was remodelled in 2012, when Guimarães was European Capital of Culture.
toural.tip: The Toural is an open square, free to visit. It is a handy place to start a walk: south to the Alfândega tower inscribed “Aqui nasceu Portugal” and on through the arcade to the squares of Santiago and Oliveira, or north to the Dukes' Palace and the castle. The square has plenty of cafés and restaurants, and a market on some weekends. Come back in the evening, when the fountain and the old façades are lit.
